html:
A treatise in ten books on building, by the Roman architect and military engineer Vitruvius, dedicated to Augustus. It is the only work on architecture to survive whole from the ancient world.

It covers far more than buildings:

  • the training of an architect and the planning of towns;
  • materials, among them lime, sand and the volcanic ash that made Roman concrete;
  • temples and the orders of columns;
  • theatres, baths, harbours and houses;
  • finding water and building aqueducts;
  • sundials, astronomy and machines, including siege engines.

Its best-known idea is that a building needs three things: strength, usefulness and beauty. Vitruvius also wrote that a well-built man with arms and legs spread fits inside a circle and a square, which Leonardo da Vinci drew as the Vitruvian Man.

Copies survived in medieval libraries, and from the 1400s it became the bible of Renaissance architects such as Alberti and Palladio, who used it to bring back classical building.
